claim: Ciliates are microbial eukaryotes that undergo extensive programmed genome rearrangement.
source: Ciliates are microbial eukaryotes that undergo extensive programmed genome rearrangement, a natural genome editing process that converts long germline chromosomes into smaller gene-rich somatic chromosomes.
evidence: This is a general statement about ciliates that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Oxytricha trifallax has a massively scrambled genome requiring hundreds of thousands of precisely programmed DNA joining events.
source: only the Oxytricha lineage has a massively scrambled genome, whose assembly during development requires hundreds of thousands of precisely programmed DNA joining events, representing the most complex genome dynamics of any known organism.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the study and prior research on Oxytricha genome rearrangement.

claim: The germline and somatic genomes of Euplotes woodruffi were sequenced, assembled, and annotated in this study.
source: We sequenced, assembled, and annotated the germline and somatic genomes of E. woodruffi, which provides an outgroup
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental work performed in the study.

claim: The germline genome of Tetmemena sp. was sequenced and assembled in this study.
source: We sequenced, assembled, and annotated the germline and somatic genomes of E. woodruffi, which provides an outgroup, and the germline genome of Tetmemena sp.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental work performed in the study.

claim: 13.6% of Tetmemena gene loci require programmed translocations and/or inversions.
source: We find that the germline genome of Tetmemena is as massively scrambled and interrupted as Oxytricha's: 13.6% of its gene loci require programmed translocations and/or inversions
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: Some genes in Tetmemena require hundreds of precise gene editing events during development.
source: 13.6% of its gene loci require programmed translocations and/or inversions, with some genes requiring hundreds of precise gene editing events during development.
evidence: This is a finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: 7.3% of E. woodruffi gene loci are scrambled.
source: This study revealed that the earlier diverged spirotrich, E. woodruffi, also has a scrambled genome, but only roughly half as many loci (7.3%) are scrambled.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: E. woodruffi scrambled genes are less complex than those in Oxytricha and Tetmemena.
source: Furthermore, its scrambled genes are less complex, together supporting the position of Euplotes as a possible evolutionary intermediate in this lineage
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of genome complexity across species.

claim: E. woodruffi represents a possible evolutionary intermediate in the accumulation of complex genome rearrangements.
source: together supporting the position of Euplotes as a possible evolutionary intermediate in this lineage, in the process of accumulating complex evolutionary genome rearrangements
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative genomic analysis showing intermediate levels of scrambling.

claim: Scrambled loci are often associated with local duplications.
source: Comparative analysis also reveals that scrambled loci are often associated with local duplications
evidence: This is a finding from comparative genomic analysis performed in the study.

claim: Local duplications support a gradual model for the origin of complex, scrambled genomes via DNA duplication and decay.
source: supporting a gradual model for the origin of complex, scrambled genomes via many small events of DNA duplication and decay.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association between scrambled loci and duplications, supporting a previously proposed model.

claim: Programmed genome editing is a naturally occurring and essential part of development in many organisms including ciliates, nematodes, lampreys, and zebra finches.
source: Programmed genome editing is a naturally occurring and essential part of development in many organisms, including ciliates (Chen et al., 2014), nematodes (Mitreva et al., 2005), lampreys (Smith et al., 2012), and zebra finches (Biederman et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Most programmed genome editing events involve precise removal and rejoining of large regions of DNA during postzygotic differentiation.
source: Most of these events involve precise removal and rejoining of large regions of DNA during postzygotic differentiation of a somatic genome from a germline genome.
evidence: This is a general statement about genome editing mechanisms supported by established knowledge.

claim: Ciliates have two types of nuclei: a somatic macronucleus (MAC) and a germline micronucleus (MIC).
source: Ciliates are microbial eukaryotes with two types of nuclei: a somatic macronucleus (MAC) that differentiates from a germline micronucleus (MIC).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliate cell biology.

claim: The Oxytricha MAC is entirely active chromatin and the hub of transcription.
source: In the model ciliate Oxytricha, the MAC is entirely active chromatin (Beh et al., 2019) and the hub of transcription.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Spirotrichs have gene-sized 'nanochromosomes' in the MAC present at high copy number.
source: The three species that we compare are all spirotrichs, which have gene-sized 'nanochromosomes' in the MAC, present at high copy number (Swart et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Lindblad et al., 2019; Vinogradov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The diploid MIC participates in sexual reproduction but its megabase-sized chromosomes are mostly transcriptionally silent.
source: The diploid MIC participates in sexual reproduction, but its megabase-sized chromosomes are mostly transcriptionally silent.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ciliate MIC function.

claim: Gene loci are often arranged discontinuously in the MIC with short genic segments (MDSs) interrupted by non-coding DNA (IESs).
source: Gene loci are often arranged discontinuously in the MIC, with short genic segments called macronuclear destined sequences (MDSs), interrupted by stretches of non-coding DNA called internally eliminated sequences (IESs) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of MIC genome structure illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: During sexual development, MDSs join in the correct order and orientation while MIC-limited genomic regions undergo programmed deletion.
source: During sexual development, a new MAC genome rearranges from a copy of the zygotic MIC genome. MDSs join in the correct order and orientation, whereas MIC-limited genomic regions undergo programmed deletion, including repetitive elements, intergenic regions, and IESs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the genome rearrangement process illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MDSs for some MAC chromosomes are scrambled if they require translocation or inversion during MAC development.
source: The MDSs for some MAC chromosomes are scrambled if they require translocation or inversion during MAC development (Figure 1A).
evidence: This defines scrambled genes with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Pairs of short repeats called pointers are present at MDS-IES junctions in both scrambled and nonscrambled loci.
source: Pairs of short repeats, called pointers, are present at MDS-IES junctions in both scrambled and nonscrambled loci (Mitcham et al., 1992; Prescott, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pointer sequences are present twice in the MIC at the end of MDS n and the beginning of MDS n+1.
source: Pointer sequences are present twice in the MIC, at the end of MDS n and the beginning of MDS n+1.
evidence: This describes the structure of pointers in the MIC genome.

claim: One copy of the pointer repeat is retained at each MDS-MDS junction in a mature MAC chromosome.
source: One copy of the repeat is retained at each MDS-MDS junction in a mature MAC chromosome (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes pointer retention during genome rearrangement, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Microhomologous pointer regions help guide MDS recombination but most are non-unique and the shortest pointers are just 2 bp.
source: These microhomologous regions help guide MDS recombination, but most are non-unique, and the shortest pointers are just 2 bp.
evidence: This describes the properties and function of pointers based on established knowledge.

claim: Thousands of long, noncoding template RNAs collectively program MDS joining.
source: Thousands of long, noncoding template RNAs collectively program MDS joining (Nowacki et al., 2008; Lindblad et al., 2017; Yerlici and Landweber, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Paramecium uses exclusively 2 bp pointers and lacks evidence of any scrambled loci.
source: Paramecium uses exclusively 2 bp pointers and lacks evidence of any scrambled loci.
evidence: This is a statement about Paramecium genome features based on established knowledge.

claim: A small number of scrambled loci (4 confirmed out of 2711 candidates) have been reported in Tetrahymena.
source: A small number of scrambled loci (4 confirmed out of 2711 candidates) have been reported in Tetrahymena (Sheng et al., 2020, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Tetrahymena and Paramecium diverged from Oxytricha over 1 billion years ago.
source: Tetrahymena and Paramecium diverged from Oxytricha over 1 billion years ago (Parfrey et al., 2011; Bracht et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior phylogenetic research.

claim: Tetmemena sp. is a hypotrich similar to Tetmemena pustulata in the same family as O. trifallax.
source: Tetmemena sp. is a hypotrich similar to Tetmemena pustulata, formerly Stylonychia pustulata (Chen et al., 2015), in the same family as O. trifallax (Figure 1B; Chen et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Hypotrichs are noted for the presence of scrambled genes based on previous ortholog comparisons.
source: Hypotrichs are noted for the presence of scrambled genes, based on previous ortholog comparisons (Chen et al., 2015; Hogan et al., 2001; Chang et al., 2005; DuBois and Prescott, 1995; Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: E. woodruffi belongs to the class Spirotrichea together with hypotrichous ciliates.
source: E. woodruffi, together with the hypotrichous ciliates, belong to the class Spirotrichea (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a taxonomic classification statement supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Euplotes has gene-sized nanochromosomes in the MAC genome.
source: Like hypotrichs, Euplotes also has gene-sized nanochromosomes in the MAC genome (Wang et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Euplotes uses a different genetic code where UGA is reassigned to cysteine.
source: this outgroup uses a different genetic code (UGA is reassigned to cysteine, Meyer et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A partial MIC genome of Euplotes vannus was previously assembled and contains highly conserved TA pointers.
source: A partial MIC genome of Euplotes vannus was previously assembled, and it contains highly conserved TA pointers (Chen et al., 2019), consistent with previous observations in Euplotes crassus (Klobutcher and Herrick, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: O. trifallax uses longer pointers of varying lengths with scrambled pointers typically longer than nonscrambled ones.
source: This differs from O. trifallax, which uses longer pointers of varying lengths, with scrambled pointers typically longer than nonscrambled ones (Chen et al., 2014, Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Longer pointers may supply more information to facilitate MDS descrambling over great distances.
source: This observation suggests that longer pointers may supply more information to facilitate MDS descrambling, sometimes over great distances.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation about pointer lengths.

claim: The preponderance of 2 bp pointers in Euplotes species could indicate limited capacity to support scrambled genes.
source: Therefore, the preponderance of 2 bp pointers in the other Euplotes species could indicate limited capacity to support scrambled genes
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between pointer length and scrambling capacity.

claim: A partial genome survey of E. vannus concluded that at least 97% of loci are nonscrambled.
source: a partial genome survey of E. vannus concluded that at least 97% of loci are nonscrambled (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Early studies of Euplotes octocarinatus demonstrated its use of longer pointers that usually contain TA.
source: Early studies of Euplotes octocarinatus, on the other hand, demonstrated its use of longer pointers (that usually contain TA) (Tan et al., 1999; Wang et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some members of the Euplotes genus may have the capacity to support complex genome reorganization.
source: suggesting that some members of the Euplotes genus may have the capacity to support complex genome reorganization.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of longer pointers in some Euplotes species.

claim: E. woodruffi is closely related to E. octocarinatus.
source: To investigate the origin of scrambled genomes, we choose E. woodruffi as an outgroup, because it is closely related to E. octocarinatus (Syberg-Olsen et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior phylogenetic research.

claim: The Tetmemena MIC genome is extremely interrupted, like Oxytricha.
source: The MIC genome of Tetmemena is extremely interrupted, like Oxytricha.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparative genomic analysis performed in the study.

claim: The E. woodruffi MIC genome is much more IES-sparse than Oxytricha and Tetmemena.
source: While the E. woodruffi MIC genome is much more IES-sparse, it contains thousands of scrambled genes
evidence: This is a finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: E. woodruffi contains thousands of scrambled genes.
source: While the E. woodruffi MIC genome is much more IES-sparse, it contains thousands of scrambled genes
evidence: This is a finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: The evolutionary origin of scrambled genes is associated with local duplications.
source: We infer that the evolutionary origin of scrambled genes is associated with local duplications
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The findings provide strong support for a previously proposed simple evolutionary model requiring only duplication and decay.
source: providing strong support for a previously proposed simple evolutionary model requiring only duplication and decay (Gao et al., 2015)
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings, supporting a model from prior research.

claim: The Tetmemena MIC genome assembly is 237 Mbp, nearly half that of Oxytricha.
source: Surprisingly, the MIC genome sizes differ substantially: the Tetmemena MIC genome assembly is 237 Mbp, nearly half that of Oxytricha.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome assembly reported in the study.

claim: The E. woodruffi MIC genome assembly is approximately 172 Mbp.
source: The E. woodruffi MIC genome assembly is even smaller, approximately 172 Mbp (Table 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome assembly reported in Table 1.

claim: The expansion of repetitive elements in the Oxytricha lineage may contribute to the difference in MIC genome sizes.
source: The expansion of repetitive elements in the Oxytricha lineage may contribute to the difference in MIC genome sizes (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of repetitive element content shown in Figure 2.

claim: Oxytricha has a variety of transposable elements (TEs) in the MIC with telomere-bearing elements (TBEs) of the Tc1/mariner family the most abundant.
source: Oxytricha has a variety of tranposable elements (TEs) in the MIC, with telomere-bearing elements (TBEs) of the Tc1/mariner family the most abundant (Chen et al., 2014; Chen and Landweber, 2016, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to supplementary data.

claim: A complete TBE transposon contains three open reading frames (ORFs).
source: A complete TBE transposon contains three open reading frames (ORFs).
evidence: This describes the structure of TBE transposons based on established knowledge.

claim: TBE ORF1 encodes a 42kD transposase with a DDE-catalytic motif.
source: ORF1 encodes a 42kD transposase with a DDE-catalytic motif.
evidence: This describes the function of TBE ORF1 based on established knowledge.

claim: The Oxytricha MIC genome contains ~10,000 complete TBEs and ~24,000 partial TBEs.
source: The Oxytricha MIC genome contains ~10,000 complete TBEs and ~24,000 partial TBEs, which occupy approximately 15.20% (75 Mbp) of the genome (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 3; Chen et al., 2014; Chen and Landweber, 2016).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis supported by citations and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Tetmemena has 48 complete TBEs comprising 1.83% (4.3 Mbp) of its MIC genome.
source: Tetmemena, on the other hand, has many fewer TBE ORFs and only 48 complete TBEs (Supplementary file 3), comprising 1.83% (4.3 Mbp) of its MIC genome (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: E. crassus has an abundant transposon family called Tec elements.
source: E. crassus has also been reported to have an abundant transposon family called Tec elements (Transposon of Euplotes crassus).
evidence: This is a statement about E. crassus transposons based on established knowledge.

claim: Each Tec element consists of three ORFs with ORF1 encoding a transposase from the Tc1/mariner family.
source: Like TBEs, each Tec consists of three ORFs, and ORF1 also encodes a transposase from the Tc1/mariner family (Baird et al., 1989; Krikau and Jahn, 1991; Jahn et al., 1993; Jahn et al., 1989; Klobutcher and Herrick, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: 74 complete Tec elements were identified in E. woodruffi.
source: Using the three ORFs of Tec1 and Tec2 as queries for search, we identified 74 complete Tec elements in E. woodruffi.
evidence: This is a finding from the genome analysis performed in the study.

claim: Tec ORFs occupy 3.6 Mbp corresponding to 2.1% of the E. woodruffi MIC genome.
source: Collectively, Tec ORFs occupy 3.6 Mbp, corresponding to only 2.1% of the MIC genome (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The transposase-encoding ORF1 is more abundant than the other two TBE/Tec ORFs in all three ciliates.
source: Notably, the transposase-encoding ORF1 is more abundant than the other two TBE/Tec ORFs in all three ciliates (Supplementary file 3)
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of ORF abundance.

claim: The abundance of ORF1 is consistent with its proposed role in DNA cleavage during genome rearrangement in Oxytricha.
source: consistent with its proposed role in DNA cleavage during genome rearrangement in Oxytricha (Nowacki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on ORF1 abundance and a citation to prior research.

claim: Only TBE3 is present in the Tetmemena MIC genome.
source: This confirmed that only TBE3 is present in the Tetmemena MIC genome, as proposed in Chen and Landweber, 2016.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis supporting a prior proposal.

claim: TBE1 and TBE2 expanded in Oxytricha after its divergence from other hypotrichous ciliates.
source: This also suggests that TBE1 and TBE2 expanded in Oxytricha after its divergence from other hypotrichous ciliates.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis of TBE families.

claim: The MIC genome contexts of TBEs in Oxytricha and Tetmemena are similar with many TE insertions within IESs.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, the MIC genome contexts of TBEs in Oxytricha and Tetmemena are similar, with many TE insertions within IESs
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: IESs may be hotspots for TE insertion or some TE insertions may have generated IESs.
source: consistent with either IESs as hotspots for TE insertion or with the model (Klobutcher and Herrick, 1997) that some TE insertions may have generated IESs, as demonstrated in Paramecium (Sellis et al., 2021; Feng and Landweber, 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on TE insertion patterns and citations to prior research.

claim: 214 Mbp of the Oxytricha MIC genome (43%) is considered repetitive.
source: 214 Mbp of the Oxytricha MIC genome (43%, which is greater than 35.9% reported in Chen et al., 2014 that used earlier versions of the software) is considered repetitive (including TBEs, tandem repeats, and other repeats in Figure 2)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from repeat analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: 31.7 Mbp (13.4%) of the Tetmemena MIC genome is repetitive.
source: versus 31.7 Mbp for Tetmemena (13.4%)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from repeat analysis.

claim: 28.5 Mbp (16.8%) of the E. woodruffi MIC genome is repetitive.
source: and 28.5 Mbp (16.8%) for E. woodruffi.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from repeat analysis.

claim: Oxytricha's additional ~180 Mbp in repeat content partially explains the significantly larger MIC genome size versus the other spirotrich ciliates.
source: Oxytricha's additional ~180 Mbp in repeat content partially explains the significantly larger MIC genome size of Oxytricha versus the other spirotrich ciliates.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis of repeat content and genome size.

claim: Over 215,299 MDSs were annotated in Oxytricha.
source: We annotated over 215,299 MDSs in Oxytricha
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome annotation.

claim: Over 215,624 MDSs were annotated in Tetmemena.
source: and over 215,624 in Tetmemena with similar MDS length distributions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome annotation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: E. woodruffi MDSs are typically longer indicating a less interrupted genome.
source: By contrast, E. woodruffi MDSs are typically longer, which indicates a less interrupted genome (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation (R2=0.75) between number of MDSs for orthologous genes in Oxytricha and Tetmemena.
source: There is a strong positive correlation between number of MDSs for orthologous genes in Oxytricha and Tetmemena (R2=0.75, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no correlation (R2=0.003) among number of MDSs between orthologs of E. woodruffi and Oxytricha.
source: There is no correlation among number of MDSs between orthologs of E. woodruffi and Oxytricha (R2=0.003, Figure 3C)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: E. woodruffi orthologs typically contain fewer MDSs than Oxytricha orthologs.
source: since E. woodruffi orthologs typically contain fewer MDSs.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of orthologous genes.

claim: 39.9% of MAC nanochromosomes in E. woodruffi lack IESs.
source: 39.9% of MAC nanochromosomes in E. woodruffi lack IESs (IES-less nanochromosomes) compared to only 4.1 and 4.4% in Oxytricha and Tetmemena, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: 4.1% of MAC nanochromosomes in Oxytricha lack IESs.
source: compared to only 4.1 and 4.4% in Oxytricha and Tetmemena, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: 4.4% of MAC nanochromosomes in Tetmemena lack IESs.
source: compared to only 4.1 and 4.4% in Oxytricha and Tetmemena, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: The sparse IES distribution in E. woodruffi displays a 5' end bias on single-gene MAC chromosomes.
source: The sparse IES distribution (as measured by plotting pointer distributions) in E. woodruffi displays a curious 5' end bias on single-gene MAC chromosomes, oriented in gene direction (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A weak 5' bias is present in Oxytricha.
source: A weak 5' bias is also present in Oxytricha (Figure 3D)
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A weak 5' bias is present in Tetmemena.
source: and Tetmemena (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: E. woodruffi IESs preferentially accumulate in the 5' UTR upstream of start codons.
source: In addition, E. woodruffi IESs preferentially accumulate in the 5' UTR, a short distance upstream of start codons (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from genome analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The median distance between the 5' telomere addition site and the start codon in E. woodruffi is 54 bp for single-gene chromosomes.
source: Notably, the median distance between the 5' telomere addition site and the start codon in E. woodruffi is just 54 bp for single-gene chromosomes, approximately half that of Oxytricha (Swart et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis with a citation to prior research.

claim: Scrambled genome rearrangements exist in all three species.
source: Scrambled genome rearrangements exist in all three species, which we report here for the first time in Tetmemena and the early diverged E. woodruffi.
evidence: This is a finding from the study reporting scrambled genes in these species for the first time.

claim: E. woodruffi contains 2429 scrambled genes encoded on 1913 chromosomes (7.3% of genes).
source: the E. woodruffi genome is scrambled, but it contains approximately half as many scrambled genes (2429 genes encoded on 1913 chromosomes, or 7.3% of genes)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: 15.6% of genes are scrambled in O. trifallax (3613 genes encoded on 2852 chromosomes).
source: versus 15.6% scrambled in O. trifallax (3613 genes encoded on 2852 chromosomes)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: 13.6% of genes are scrambled in Tetmemena (3371 genes encoded on 2556 chromosomes).
source: and 13.6% in Tetmemena (3371 genes encoded on 2556 chromosomes).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: The E. woodruffi lineage may reflect an evolutionary intermediate stage between ancestral genomes with modest levels of genome scrambling and the more massively scrambled genomes of hypotrichs.
source: The E. woodruffi lineage may therefore reflect an evolutionary intermediate stage between ancestral genomes with only modest levels of genome scrambling and the more massively scrambled genomes of hypotrichs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the intermediate level of scrambling observed in E. woodruffi.

claim: Oxytricha and Tetmemena share approximately half of their scrambled genes.
source: We infer that many genes were likely scrambled in the last common ancestor of Oxytricha and Tetmemena, because these two species share approximately half of their scrambled genes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis supporting an inference about ancestral scrambling.

claim: Most scrambled genes are not new genes since they possess at least one ortholog in other ciliate species.
source: Furthermore, most scrambled genes are not new genes, since they possess at least one ortholog in other ciliate species (Supplementary file 4, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from ortholog analysis.

claim: Scrambled genes in all three species generally have more paralogs.
source: Notably, scrambled genes in all three species generally have more paralogs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Orthogroups with at least one scrambled gene are significantly larger than those containing no scrambled genes (p-value <1e−5) in all three species.
source: For each species, orthogroups with at least one scrambled gene are significantly larger than those containing no scrambled genes (p-value <1e−5, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The association between scrambled genes and larger orthogroups suggests a possible role of gene duplication in the origin of scrambled genes.
source: This association suggests a possible role of gene duplication in the origin of scrambled genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed association between scrambling and paralogy.

claim: Scrambled pointers are generally longer than nonscrambled ones in all three species.
source: Scrambled pointers are generally longer than nonscrambled ones in all three species (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Scrambled 'pointers' in E. woodruffi can be as long as several hundred base pairs (median 48 bp, average 212 bp).
source: Curiously, scrambled 'pointers' in E. woodruffi can be as long as several hundred base pairs (median 48 bp, average 212 bp)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from genome analysis.

claim: Long 'pointers' in E. woodruffi are more likely partial MDS duplications.
source: These long 'pointers' in E. woodruffi are more likely partial MDS duplications (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the length of pointers shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There are significantly more scrambled chromosomes than nonscrambled MAC chromosomes that contain at least one paralogous MDS (chi-square test, p-value <1e−10) in all three species.
source: Moreover, we find that, for all three species, there are significantly more scrambled chromosomes than nonscrambled MAC chromosomes that contain at least one paralogous MDS (chi-square test, p-value <1e−10; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis.

claim: The presence of paralogous MDSs can contribute to the origin of scrambled rearrangements as proposed by Gao et al., 2015.
source: The presence of paralogous MDSs can contribute to the origin of scrambled rearrangements, as proposed in an elegant model by Gao et al., 2015; illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings supporting a model from prior research.

claim: For 248 MDS-IES pairs of similar length in E. woodruffi, 90.3% share a core sequence with ~97.5% identity across 8–100% of both the IES and MDS length.
source: Moreover, many MDS and IES sequence pairs also share sequence similarity, consistent with paralogy: for 248 MDS-IES pairs of similar length, 90.3% share a core sequence with ~97.5% identity across 8–100% of both the IES and MDS length.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The lengths of MDS/IES pairs in E. woodruffi strongly correlate (Spearman correlation ρ=0.755, p<1e−5).
source: In E. woodruffi, the lengths of these MDS/IES pairs strongly correlate (Spearman correlation ρ=0.755, p<1e−5, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The odd-even-containing loci that are species-specific have the strongest length correlation between MDS and IES pairs.
source: Remarkably, the odd-even-containing loci that are species-specific, and therefore became scrambled more recently, have the strongest length correlation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–E)
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Species-specific scrambled loci have more pairs that display sequence similarity relative to older loci.
